title: Reverse Pairs
spaceBreakdown:
- vector<int> tmp inside mergeSort: up to n elements at the top level → O(n)
- recursion call-stack depth: balanced merge-sort tree, O(log n)
- not counted: input nums (modified in place), returned int
approach: Use merge sort: recursively sort the two halves while counting reverse pairs fully inside each half. After both halves are sorted, count cross pairs (i in left, j in right) with a single advancing pointer j, because for sorted left and right halves, the threshold nums[i] > 2·nums[j] is monotonic in both i and j. Then merge the two sorted halves in place. All comparisons use `long long` to avoid overflow when doubling INT_MIN/INT_MAX.
hints: With n up to 5·10^4, all ~1.25·10^9 pairs cannot be checked individually. Suppose you split the array into two halves and already knew every reverse pair lying fully inside each half - what property would the two halves need so that counting cross pairs (i in left, j in right) takes linear time?

Use merge sort: recursively sort each half, count cross pairs with one advancing pointer over the sorted right half, then merge. For nums=[1,3,2,3,1], after sorting left=[1,2,3] and right=[1,3], only nums[i]=3 advances j past nums[j]=1 (3>2), adding 1 cross pair.

```
function count(lo, hi):
    if lo >= hi: return 0
    mid = (lo + hi) / 2
    ans = count(lo, mid) + count(mid+1, hi)
    j = mid + 1
    for i in lo..mid:
        while j <= hi and nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]:
            j = j + 1
        ans += j - (mid + 1)
    merge sorted nums[lo..mid] with nums[mid+1..hi]
    return ans
```

**Single element** - n = 1, no pair possible.
`Input: [5]` → `Expected: 0`
⚠️ Bug: omitting the `lo >= hi` base case and reading `nums[mid+1]` → out-of-bounds access / crash.

**INT_MAX doubling** - 2·(2^31−1) exceeds int range.
`Input: [2147483647, 2147483647]` → `Expected: 0`
⚠️ Bug: writing `nums[i] > 2 * nums[j]` with int arithmetic → 2·2147483647 wraps to −2, comparison is true → returns 1.

**INT_MIN doubling** - 2·(−2^31) also overflows int.
`Input: [-2147483648, -2147483648]` → `Expected: 1`
⚠️ Bug: `2 * nums[j]` as int wraps to 0, so −2147483648 > 0 is false → returns 0.

**All equal negatives** - equal values still satisfy x > 2x when x < 0.
`Input: [-1, -1, -1]` → `Expected: 3`
⚠️ Bug: skipping pairs where nums[i] == nums[j] → returns 0.

followUps.q: The array arrives as an unbounded stream and cannot be stored. How do you count reverse pairs online?
followUps.a: Process elements right-to-left, inserting each into a balanced BST (or Fenwick tree over value compression). For each new nums[i], query how many already-inserted values are < nums[i]/2. TC O(n log n), SC O(n) for the structure.

followUps.q: Generalise to nums[i] > k·nums[j] for an arbitrary positive constant k (possibly fractional).
followUps.a: Same merge-sort skeleton; replace `2LL * nums[j]` with `k * nums[j]` computed in double or long long. Monotonicity of the advancing j pointer is preserved because k > 0 keeps k·nums[j] monotonic in sorted nums[j]. TC O(n log n), SC O(n).

followUps.q: Return every reverse pair (i, j) instead of just the count.
followUps.a: The output itself can be Θ(n^2) (e.g., all elements equal to −1), so no sub-quadratic bound is possible. Collect pairs during the counting pass of merge sort, enumerating each valid j for each i. TC O(n log n + P) where P is the number of pairs, SC O(n + P).
